## Goals

* Introduce/review the classic package development workflow
* Introduce key AI-powered workflows

## The classic workflow

The classic workflow is unchanged:

1. Write a function in `R/`
1. `load_all()` (⌘⇧L) and try it in the console
1. Write tests with `use_test()`
1. `test()` (⌘⇧T) and iterate until they passc
1. `document()` (⌘⇧D) to update docs
1. `check()` (⌘⇧E) at the end

(Windows/Linux: use Ctrl instead of ⌘)

The AI just does more of the typing; you still own the loop

## Your turn {.your-turn}

Try out the workflow with your compliments package.

* Start with a fresh Positron instance, and confirm you can't run your `compliments()` function.
* Run `devtools::load_all()` or use the keyboard shortcut and confirm that you can. Make a simple change, re-load, re-run and check that you see it.
* 

## What changes with AI

* You describe the function; the agent writes it
* You still run `load_all()` and play with the result — this is your most important feedback
* Ask the agent to write tests, but review them carefully
* Let the agent iterate on `test()` failures
* `check()` stays the final gate

## General principles

* You are still important and still in control!
* Choose what to invest in (e.g. code, tests, planning, design, docs)
* Start slow and grow your confidence
* Never make another human read AI slop

## AI workflows

<!-- TODO: make a diagram for this -->

* Implement it
* Plan it, then implement it
* Plan it, review the plan, implement it, review the implementation
* Design it, then repeat cycles above

## Basic advice

* When you get started, pay attention to what it's doing
* Can be useful to intervene when it's getting off track
* Can also be useful to let it run, smacking its head into the wall again and again and again until it eventually figures it out

## Git flow

* When you get started, I think it's worth doing all the commits yourself
* Then, tell it when to commit
* Then, it let it commit by itself 
* Then, let it make the whole PR
* (But NEVER EVER inflect Claude's writing on another human)

# Medium-stakes tasks

> An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure

## Now it's time to make a plan

* Planning tends to lead to better results, but don't get hung up on it
* Always ask for a markdown file that you can read and edit
* Three options for where to put this:
  * Ephemeral
  * Persistent, outside of git
  * Checked in

## Example workflow

> Read https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/2334. 
> Construct a minimal reprex, then write a brief plan for fixing the problem.
> Save your plan in plan.md.

... read and review the plan ...

> Execute the plan

## Example workflow (voice)

Fine to dump a stream of consciousness and let the agent figure it out. I think it's good to ask for a plan just to check it's clear what you actually want.


# High-stakes tasks

## Workflow lore

* Claude (esp. Fable/Opus) best at planning
* Codex best at reviewing
* Cheap models fine for implementing

## Example workflow

1. Plan it with Fable (or whatever the best model you have access to is)
1. You read and review the plan
1. Review the plan with Codex. Copy and paste the feedback.
1. Implement with Sonnet (or a similar cheap model)
1. Review the implementation with Codex

> https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/2328
